# Hardware-Accelerated Simulated Radiography (Non-Emissive)

Also called: Hexahedral/Tetrahedral decomposition radiography, Layer-rendering algorithm, P-buffer accumulation, Unsorted Layer-Rendering Algorithm

## Overview
A GPU-based volume rendering technique for non-emissive objects that simulates X-ray radiography by accumulating attenuation coefficients in a floating-point off-screen P-buffer (accumulation buffer) [S1, unofficial]. It renders geometric cells (hexahedra or tetrahedra) as separate layers, using hardware-accelerated rasterization to compute the integral of attenuation along viewing rays [S1, unofficial]. Unlike sorted front-to-back methods, this algorithm handles unsorted, overlapping geometry by iteratively rendering non-overlapping subsets of cells, minimizing expensive P-buffer-to-texture synchronization copies [S1, unofficial].

## How it works
**Inputs:**
* A volume [decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md) into geometric cells (primarily hexahedra, subdivided into tetrahedra if necessary) [S1, unofficial].
* Material properties for each cell, including density $\rho$ and elemental composition [S1, unofficial].
* X-ray source spectrum, discretized into $N$ energy bands (typically $N=4$) [S1, unofficial].
* Target image resolution (e.g., $512 \times 512$) [S1, unofficial].

**Outputs:**
* An attenuation image or simulated X-ray intensity image [S1, unofficial].

**Data Structures:**
* **Attenuation Table:** Precomputed lookup table mapping material mixtures and energy bands to extinction coefficients $\kappa_\nu$ [S1, unofficial].
* **Cell List:** A logically circular list of pointers to all cells, traversed in a specific order [S1, unofficial].
* **Bounding Boxes:** For each cell, the 2D image-plane bounding box of its projection [S1, unofficial].
* **P-buffer:** A floating-point off-screen framebuffer (texture) used to accumulate attenuation values. It has $N$ channels (e.g., [RGBA](#5142-color-packing-rgba.md)) to store attenuation for $N$ energy bands in parallel [S1, unofficial].
* **Test Buffer:** A 1-bit per pixel buffer (represented in multi-bit words aligned per scan line) used to track which pixels have been covered by cells rendered in the current pass [S1, unofficial].
* **Current Texture:** A texture holding the accumulated attenuation from previous passes, used as input for interpolation [S1, unofficial].

**Formulas:**
The attenuation for a cell is computed based on the extinction coefficient and the path length through the cell [S1, unofficial]:
$$ A = K_\nu \cdot t $$
where $K_\nu$ is the extinction coefficient for energy band $\nu$, and $t$ is the thickness of the cell along the viewing ray [S1, unofficial].

The extinction coefficient $K_\nu$ is defined as [S1, unofficial]:
$$ K_\nu = \kappa \rho $$
where $\kappa$ is the opacity in $\text{cm}^2/\text{g}$ and $\rho$ is the density of the material [S1, unofficial].

The final X-ray intensity $I$ is derived from the total accumulated attenuation $A_{total}$ (sum of $A$ across all cells and bands) [S1, unofficial]:
$$ I = e^{-A_{total}} $$
This exponential is applied during the final copy to the output buffer [S1, unofficial].

**Parameters:**
* **Number of energy bands:** 4 (mapped to RGBA channels) [S1, unofficial].
* **Resolution:** Typically $512 \times 512$ or similar [S1, unofficial].
* **Threshold for pass termination:** A fixed number of skipped cells due to overlap [S1, unofficial].

**Algorithm Steps:**
1. **Preprocessing:** Read in volume data and compute the attenuation table for the specified energy bands and materials [S1, unofficial]. For each cell, compute its 2D image-plane bounding box [S1, unofficial]. If a hexahedron cannot be projected as a whole (e.g., due to non-convexity or self-intersection), subdivide it into five tetrahedra [S1, unofficial]. Form a logically circular list of pointers to all cells [S1, unofficial].
2. **Initialization:** Initialize the P-buffer to zero [G]. Initialize the Current Texture with the P-buffer data [G].
3. **Iterative Rendering Passes:** Traverse the cell list in jumps of a size relatively prime to the list's length to ensure every cell is touched once before repetition and adjacent cells are not touched consecutively [S1, unofficial]. For each cell in the traversal, clear the 1-bit Test Buffer at the start of the pass [S1, unofficial]. Scan-convert the cell's bounding box into the Test Buffer format [S1, unofficial]. The pattern along a scan line consists of a left partly filled word (from a lookup table), zero or more full words, and a right partly filled word (from a lookup table) [S1, unofficial]. Test the words involved in the bounding box against the Test Buffer using bitwise logical ANDs [S1, unofficial]. If any result is non-zero, there is overlap with a cell already rendered in the current pass; skip this cell [S1, unofficial]. If no overlap, use bitwise logical ORs to set the bits for the bounding box in the Test Buffer, mark the cell as completed in the list, and proceed to render [S1, unofficial]. Compute the attenuation for the current cell in software using geometry and $K_\nu \cdot t$ [S1, unofficial]. Interpolate the accumulated attenuation for the current cell from the Current Texture using hardware vertex [data interpolation](#7180-data-interpolation.md) [S1, unofficial]. Write the floating-point sum (accumulated attenuation) to the P-buffer [S1, unofficial]. If a threshold number of cells are skipped due to overlap, terminate the current pass [S1, unofficial]. Copy the smallest rectangle in the P-buffer containing all rendered bounding boxes into the Current Texture [S1, unofficial]. Start the next pass [S1, unofficial].
4. **Final Output:** When no cells are left (all cells rendered), copy the P-buffer (which contains the sum of all passes) to the output buffer [S1, unofficial]. If an X-ray image is desired, compute the negative exponential $e^{-A_{total}}$ during this final copy [S1, unofficial]. Draw the texture to the screen [S1, unofficial].

**Pseudocode:**
> **Unverified code.** The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors.

```python
import math

def hardware_accelerated_radiography(cells, energy_bands, resolution, output_type='attenuation'):
    # Preprocessing
    attenuation_table = compute_attenuation_table(cells, energy_bands)
    cell_list = list(cells)
    list_length = len(cell_list)
    jump_size = find_relatively_prime_number(list_length)
    
    # Initialize P-buffer (floating-point off-screen buffer)
    width, height = resolution
    channels = len(energy_bands)
    p_buffer = [[0.0] * channels for _ in range(height * width)]
    current_texture = [row[:] for row in p_buffer]
    
    # Iterative passes
    while any(not cell.completed for cell in cell_list):
        test_buffer = [0] * (width * height)
        skipped_count = 0
        threshold = 100
        
        for i in range(0, list_length, jump_size):
            cell = cell_list[i % list_length]
            if cell.completed:
                continue
                
            bbox = cell.image_plane_bounding_box
            has_overlap = False
            for y in range(bbox.y_min, bbox.y_max):
                for x in range(bbox.x_min, bbox.x_max):
                    if test_buffer[y * width + x] & 1:
                        has_overlap = True
                        break
                if has_overlap: break
            if has_overlap:
                skipped_count += 1
                continue
                
            for y in range(bbox.y_min, bbox.y_max):
                for x in range(bbox.x_min, bbox.x_max):
                    test_buffer[y * width + x] |= 1
                    
            # Compute vertex attenuation in software
            K_nu = attenuation_table[cell.id]
            thickness = compute_thickness(cell)
            vertex_attenuation = {band: K_nu[band] * thickness for band in energy_bands}
            
            # Hardware interpolation of vertex data into P-buffer
            accumulate_to_p_buffer(p_buffer, cell.vertices, vertex_attenuation, channels, width)
            
            cell.completed = True
            
            if skipped_count > threshold:
                break
                
        rendered_rect = find_min_rect_rendered_cells(cell_list, width)
        copy_region_to_texture(p_buffer, current_texture, rendered_rect, width)
        
    if output_type == 'xray':
        output_buffer = apply_exponential(p_buffer)
    else:
        output_buffer = p_buffer
        
    draw_texture(output_buffer)

def compute_attenuation_table(cells, energy_bands):
    table = {}
    for cell in cells:
        table[cell.id] = {}
        for band in energy_bands:
            kappa = get_opacity(cell.material, band)
            rho = cell.density
            table[cell.id][band] = kappa * rho
    return table

def find_relatively_prime_number(n):
    for j in range(2, n):
        if math.gcd(j, n) == 1:
            return j
    return 1

def compute_thickness(cell):
    return cell.path_length

def accumulate_to_p_buffer(p_buffer, vertices, vertex_attenuation, channels, width):
    bbox = get_bounding_box(vertices)
    for y in range(bbox.y_min, bbox.y_max):
        for x in range(bbox.x_min, bbox.x_max):
            for c in range(channels):
                p_buffer[y * width + x][c] += vertex_attenuation[energy_bands[c]]

def find_min_rect_rendered_cells(cell_list, width):
    min_x, min_y = float('inf'), float('inf')
    max_x, max_y = float('-inf'), float('-inf')
    for cell in cell_list:
        if cell.completed:
            bbox = cell.image_plane_bounding_box
            min_x = min(min_x, bbox.x_min)
            min_y = min(min_y, bbox.y_min)
            max_x = max(max_x, bbox.x_max)
            max_y = max(max_y, bbox.y_max)
    return {'x_min': min_x, 'y_min': min_y, 'x_max': max_x, 'y_max': max_y}

def copy_region_to_texture(p_buffer, current_texture, rect, width):
    for y in range(rect['y_min'], rect['y_max']):
        for x in range(rect['x_min'], rect['x_max']):
            current_texture[y * width + x] = p_buffer[y * width + x][:]

def apply_exponential(p_buffer):
    output = [[0.0] * len(p_buffer[0]) for _ in range(len(p_buffer))]
    for y in range(len(p_buffer)):
        for x in range(len(p_buffer[0])):
            for c in range(len(p_buffer[0])):
                output[y][x][c] = math.exp(-p_buffer[y][x][c])
    return output

def draw_texture(texture):
    pass
```

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
* **Read-before-write artifacts:** If the same framebuffer object is used for reading and writing, texture data may be used before it has been written out [S1, unofficial]. This is handled by drawing a dummy textured square (e.g., $120 \times 120$ pixels) to flush the pipeline [S1, unofficial].
* **Subdivision:** Subdividing hexahedra into tetrahedra increases depth complexity, requiring more passes [S1, unofficial].
* **Bounding Box vs. Actual Projection:** Scanning the actual projection of the cell instead of its bounding box was tested but rejected because the extra cost of stepping along the edges balanced the speed-up from fewer layers, resulting in no net gain [S1, unofficial].

## Operating characteristics
* **Time Complexity:** The method is bottlenecked by overlap determination and texture copying [S1, unofficial]. The number of passes is related to the depth complexity of the volume decomposition [S1, unofficial].
* **Memory Complexity:** Requires storage for the P-buffer, Current Texture, Test Buffer, and attenuation table [S1, unofficial].
* **Measured Performance:** On a dual processor 860 MHz Pentium4 Xeon PC with an nVidia 6800 GT graphics card, rendering 141,960 hexahedral cells (with some subdivided) at $512 \times 512$ resolution took 2.2 seconds for preprocessing and 35 seconds for rendering and copying [S1, unofficial]. Using the same framebuffer object for read/write reduced rendering time to 7.4 seconds [S1, unofficial].
* **Strengths:** Hardware-accelerated rasterization; parallel accumulation of multiple energy bands; handles unsorted, overlapping geometry without sorting [S1, unofficial].
* **Limitations:** Bottlenecked by overlap determination and texture copying; requires multiple passes for complex scenes; subdivision increases depth complexity [S1, unofficial].
* **When to use:** When simulating X-ray radiography for non-emissive volumes with complex, overlapping geometry on hardware that supports floating-point framebuffers and efficient rasterization [S1, unofficial].
* **When not to use:** When real-time performance is critical and the scene has high depth complexity; when emission is present (requires different model) [S1, unofficial].

## Background
* **Origin:** Developed for simulating X-ray radiography in high-energy density physics experiments, such as hohlraum and capsule simulations [S1, unofficial].
* **History:** Validated against software raytrace packages used by scientists for simulation [S1, unofficial]. The method uses EPDL database for atomic cross-sections [S1, unofficial].
* **Usage:** Used in scientific visualization for [absorption-only](#828-absorption-only-model.md) radiographs of complex geometries [S1, unofficial].
